questions.question: What changes, and what stays fixed, when testing commutativity of $\star$?
options: The parentheses around three inputs change, in every case without exception.
The order of the two inputs changes; the operation and the two elements stay the same.
The set changes from $A$ to $A\times A$.
The operation changes from $\star$ to addition.

questions.question: Does commutativity say anything about parentheses in $a\star b\star c$?
options: No, because commutative operations cannot be binary.
Yes, but only when $a=b=c$.
No. Parentheses are governed by associativity.
Yes. Commutativity is exactly the law of parentheses.

questions.question: Why is matrix multiplication a useful warning example for commutativity?
options: Matrix multiplication always has no identity matrix.
Matrix multiplication is never associative.
Matrix multiplication is not a binary operation on square matrices.
Even when both products exist, $AB$ and $BA$ can be different.

questions.question: What extra word is used for a group whose operation is commutative?
options: Abelian.
Singular.
Idempotent.
Defective.

questions.question: If an operation fails commutativity, what must exist?
options: No identity element in the set.
At least one pair $a,b$ with $a\star b\ne b\star a$.
No output for some ordered pair.
At least one triple with different parenthesisations.

questions.question: Which ordinary operation on real numbers is commutative?
options: Division.
Exponentiation.
Addition.
Subtraction.

questions.question: Which calculation shows that subtraction on $\mathbb R$ is not commutative?
Let $a\star b=a+b+ab$ on $\mathbb R$. Is $\star$ commutative?
options: No, because multiplication appears.
Only when $a$ and $b$ are both positive.
No, because the expression has two inputs.
Yes, because $a+b+ab=b+a+ba$.

questions.question: Let $a\star b=2a+b$ on $\mathbb R$. Which pair shows noncommutativity?
options: $1\star3=5$ but $3\star1=7$.
$0\star0=0$ but $0\star0=1$.
$1\star3=7$ but $3\star1=7$.
$1\star1=3$ but $1\star1=3$.

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, what does $AB\ne BA$ illustrate?
options: Square matrices cannot be multiplied.
Matrix multiplication is not generally commutative.
The identity matrix does not exist.
Matrix multiplication is not associative.

questions.question: For a finite operation table, what visual pattern suggests commutativity?
options: Every entry on the diagonal is the identity.
The table is upper triangular.
Every row is identical.
The table is symmetric across the main diagonal.

questions.question: Can an operation be associative but not commutative?
options: No. Associativity always implies commutativity.
Yes. Matrix multiplication is a standard example.
No. A binary operation must be both or neither.
Yes, but only if it has no identity.

questions.question: Does commutativity require an identity element to exist first?
options: Yes. Commutativity is defined using the identity element.
Yes, because $e\star a=a\star e$ is the only pair checked.
No. It only compares $a\star b$ and $b\star a$.
No, because commutativity only applies to inverse elements.

questions.question: On $\mathbb R$, is $a\star b=\max(a,b)$ commutative?
options: Yes, because $\max(a,b)=\max(b,a)$.
No, because maximum is not associative.
Only if $a,b$ are integers.
No, because maximum has no two inputs.

questions.question: If an operation table on $\{x,y\}$ has $x\star y=x$ and $y\star x=y$, what can be concluded?
options: The operation is automatically commutative.
The operation is not commutative unless $x=y$.
The operation is not a binary operation.
The operation must be associative.

questions.question: For functions $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=2x$, which equality fails?
options: $g\circ g$ is defined.
$f\circ g=g\circ f$ in general.
$(f\circ g)\circ f=f\circ(g\circ f)$.
$f\circ f$ is defined.

questions.question: Why is an Abelian group a special kind of group rather than just another name for group?
options: Abelian means associative but without inverses.
Every group is commutative by definition.
Abelian means the identity element is missing.
Groups do not have to be commutative.

questions.question: Why is checking only $a\star a=a\star a$ useless for commutativity?
options: It checks associativity instead.
It checks that no identity exists.
It never compares two different orders.
It disproves commutativity immediately.

questions.question: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. What are $AB$ and $BA$?
options: Both products are the zero matrix.
Both products are the identity matrix, regardless of the specific input chosen.
$AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
$AB=BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.question: On $\mathbb Z$, define $a\star b=a+b+2ab$. Is $\star$ commutative?
options: No, because $2ab$ makes the operation noncommutative.
Yes, because the formula is symmetric in $a$ and $b$.
Only when one of the inputs is zero.
No, because integers are not closed under the rule.
